title: Cafe / small restaurant input-cost shock
description: Behavioural slice for a single cafe facing an ingredient/input cost increase and choosing a pricing and menu response. Daily resolution. The module carries ONLY the causal/behavioural relationships, in index space (100 = pre-shock normal). Revenue, gross profit and cash are accounting identities over these trajectories and are computed by event_sim.cafe.accounting, never by edges - a margin or a cash balance is not a state that relaxes toward a pressure.
notes: DESIGN AUDIT (2026-08-20). The engine relaxes every non-stock variable toward a linear pressure and offers one stock rule, a capacity-bounded queue. Neither can represent an accounting identity (gross profit = revenue - COGS) or an integrator (cash += net cash flow). Putting those in the module would smear a definition across time and double-count. They are therefore excluded from the module by design and computed deterministically from the module's output. Everything that IS here is a behavioural response with a lag: purchasing passes input cost into COGS over about a week of inventory; customers respond to a price change over a couple of weeks. EVIDENCE: the price->demand edge is literature_backed at its central setting (Andreyeva, Long & Brownell 2010, AJPH, food-away-from-home category elasticity 0.81, 95% CI 0.56-1.07) and the high setting is an expert_assumption placed between that CI's top and the brand-level meta-analytic mean of 2.62 (Bijmolt, van Heerde & Pieters 2005, JMR), because a single outlet raising prices while competitors hold theirs faces substitution the category estimate does not capture. Every other coefficient is an expert_assumption and says so.

variables.label: Supplier / ingredient price level
variables.observability_note: The owner sees this directly on supplier invoices. The shock event holds it.
variables.description: What the cafe pays its suppliers per unit of ingredients, relative to before the shock. Held by the cost-shock event for the whole horizon: a cost increase is a stated fact, not a pressure to relax away from.

variables.label: Ingredient cost per order
variables.observability_note: Observable from the owner's purchase ledger divided by order count, with a lag: ingredients already on the shelf were bought at the old price.
variables.description: Average ingredient cost embedded in one order. Rises toward the new input price as old inventory is used up (response 0.25/day ~ a 2-3 day half-life on top of the 7-day edge lag). World C's menu reformulation lowers it by a fixed number of index points.

variables.label: Average menu price
variables.observability_note: Set by the owner. No incoming edges: it moves only when an intervention moves it.
variables.description: Average price charged per order relative to before the shock. A decision variable, not an outcome: it has no incoming edges and holds exactly the intervention offset.

variables.label: Customer orders
variables.observability_note: Daily order count from the till.
variables.description: Daily orders relative to before the shock. Responds to the menu price through the elasticity edge, gradually: response 0.05/day means customers reach half of their full reaction in about two weeks. That speed is an assumption and is swept.

edges.mechanism: Ingredient purchases are the cafe's cost of goods. A supplier increase lands in COGS once inventory bought at the old price is consumed (~a week for fresh stock). Central pass-through is 1.0 by definition of the input; the low setting represents partial substitution, renegotiation or hedged contracts absorbing some of it. Pass-through above 1.0 is not modelled.

evidence.reference: Andreyeva T, Long MW, Brownell KD. The impact of food prices on consumption: a systematic review of research on the price elasticity of demand for food. Am J Public Health. 2010;100(2):216-222. doi:10.2105/AJPH.2008.151415
evidence.note: Food away from home: mean own-price elasticity 0.81 (95% CI 0.56-1.07; range 0.23-1.76) across 13 US estimates, studies 1938-2007. CATEGORY-level: describes demand for eating out as a whole when the whole category's price moves. Supports the CENTRAL setting for a cost shock that hits the whole local market, so competitors raise too.

evidence.reference: Bijmolt THA, van Heerde HJ, Pieters RGM. New empirical generalizations on the determinants of price elasticity. J Marketing Res. 2005;42(2):141-156.
evidence.note: Mean BRAND-level price elasticity -2.62 across 1,851 estimates from 81 studies, predominantly packaged goods in scanner data. Cited as the reference point for a single outlet raising prices while competitors hold theirs; NOT transferred directly, because an independent cafe is differentiated by location and habit in ways a supermarket brand is not. The HIGH setting (1.60) is an expert judgement between the category CI top (1.07) and this mean, and is labelled expert_assumption.

edges.mechanism: Customers buy fewer orders, trade down, or go elsewhere when the average price rises. Coefficient is the own-price elasticity magnitude: a 1% price rise eventually reduces orders by that percentage. The lag is 0 because the reaction begins at once; how fast it completes is the demand variable's response rate, not the edge.

axes.label: How price-sensitive are your customers?
axes.description: The single assumption most likely to change the decision. Low: loyal customers and competitors raising too (0.50). Central: the food-away-from-home category estimate (0.81, literature). High: you raise, competitors hold, customers have an easy alternative (1.60, expert judgement).

axes.label: How much of the supplier increase reaches your cost of goods?
axes.description: Low: you absorb some through substitution, renegotiation or contracts (0.70). Central and high: all of it (1.00).

axes.label: How quickly do customers react?
axes.description: Multiplies the demand response rate. Slow: half-reaction in about a month. Central: about two weeks. Fast: about a week.

interventions.label: Raise average menu prices
interventions.description: Adds the given number of percentage points to the average menu price for the whole horizon. Magnitude is the price increase in percent.

interventions.label: Remove or reformulate low-margin items
interventions.description: Lowers average ingredient cost per order by the given number of percentage points of the pre-shock COGS, and costs a small share of orders from customers who came for the removed items. Magnitude is the COGS reduction in percentage points; the demand cost is a fixed ratio of it (expert assumption, see evidence registry).

observability_note: Every variable in this module is observable or proxy-observable by the cafe owner from their own till and purchase ledger. That is deliberate: a decision tool whose inputs the customer cannot see is a tool the customer cannot check.
